summary: Describes the DISCOVER opcode, an experimental DNS extension that used multicast queries for resource discovery. It was tested in 1995 and 1996 for the Topology Based Domain Search project, which is no longer active. It is historic.

eli5.summary: Long ago, people tried a way to shout to the whole neighborhood to find things instead of asking one phone book. The experiment ended. It is historic.

questions: how does multicast dns discovery work
subtitle: An experimental DNS opcode for multicast resource discovery in disconnected networks.

tldr.problem: DNS normally relies on unicast queries to fixed root servers and hierarchical zones, which breaks when networks become disconnected or when devices need to discover services on a local network without being delegated a zone.
tldr.mechanism: The DISCOVER opcode allows nodes to send multicast DNS queries to find authoritative servers and services within a local scope. A client sends a DISCOVER query to a multicast address and processes multiple responses from multiple responders, rather than expecting a single reply like normal DNS QUERY.
tldr.outcome: The Topology Based Domain Search (TBDS) project tested this idea from 1995 to 1996 and successfully demonstrated multicast DNS discovery. However, TBDS is no longer active, and this work was never standardized into the DNS specification. The document is Historic.

facts.label: First multicast DNS
facts.value: Yes, TBDS was the first known use

today: RFC 6804 is Historic. The TBDS project ended in the 1990s and this work was never standardized into the DNS specification. However, the concepts influenced later multicast DNS developments and resource discovery mechanisms.

sections.title: DISCOVER and Multicast DNS
sections.content:
RFC 6804 documents the DISCOVER opcode, an experimental extension to the Domain Name System (DNS) for multicast queries and resource discovery. The Topology Based Domain Search (TBDS) project, funded under DARPA, developed and tested DISCOVER from 1995 to 1996 to enable autonomous, mobile nodes in disconnected or poorly connected networks to find services and resolvers without relying on a connection to the Internet root servers.

Unlike standard DNS QUERY, which sends a unicast request to a specific server and expects a single reply, DISCOVER sends a multicast message and anticipates receiving multiple responses from multiple authoritative servers within the local scope. This allows clients to discover the closest authoritative servers and services dynamically.

The RFC notes that TBDS was the first known use of multicast transport for DNS. While TBDS is no longer active and the work was never incorporated into the DNS specification, the concepts are historically significant in early multicast deployment research.
sections.eli5: Regular internet directories ask one phone book. DISCOVER shouts to all computers in a neighborhood at once and collects answers from whoever can help. Scientists tested this in the 1990s. It worked but the project stopped.

sections.title: DISCOVER Processing Rules
sections.content:
A DISCOVER query is sent to a multicast address with a particular multicast scope. Unlike a unicast QUERY, the requester must be prepared to receive multiple replies from multiple responders. DISCOVER responses have the same format as standard DNS responses, with Answer, Authority, and Additional sections.

DISCOVER differs from QUERY in several key ways. The Question section normally contains <QNAME=zonename,QTYPE=SOA> tuples asking about Zones of Authority, and optionally <QNAME=service,QTYPE=SRV> tuples for service discovery. If QDCOUNT is zero (no questions), only recursive servers should answer; otherwise, only authoritative servers for the queried zones should respond. This ensures that replies are always either authoritative or have the Recursion Available flag set.

Responses are sent back to the unicast address of the requester, and the responder uses its own unicast address as the source. Unlike unicast DNS, the receiver must handle multiple independent resource record sets and apply heuristics to select the most appropriate answer.
sections.eli5: You shout a question to the multicast address and computers that know the answer shout back to you. Different computers might give different answers, and you pick the best one.

sections.title: Using DISCOVER for Service Discovery
sections.content:
To perform a hostname lookup using DISCOVER, a node first computes the zone name of the reverse DNS tree (in-addr.arpa, ip6.int, or ip6.arpa), then DISCOVERs whether any in-scope servers are authoritative for that zone. If so, it queries those servers for the name; if not, it DISCOVERs recursive servers.

For service lookup, a node first performs hostname and reverse hostname discovery to find local authoritative servers, then computes the SRV service name using a wildcard: _service._transport.*.parentdomain. When DISCOVER is used with wildcard labels, the wildcard matches any label for which the DNS server is authoritative, allowing for more flexible local service discovery.

DISCOVER also enables discovery in completely disconnected networks where no external authoritative servers exist. Hosts can run a stub authoritative server that acts as though the host's fully qualified domain name is a zone. The stub server advertises itself as authoritative for its own name and provides glue records pointing to the host's link-local address. This allows peer-to-peer resource discovery without any centralized infrastructure.
sections.eli5: To find someone's address, you ask if any computers know the reverse address list. To find a service like a printer, you ask for servers near you that offer that service. You can even let your computer say it is its own zone when the network is cut off from everything else.

sections.title: Security and Limitations
sections.content:
RFC 6804 notes that multicast DNS queries have potential security risks that were not fully understood at the time of writing (early 1995-1996). The primary concerns are denial-of-service attacks through flooding and the possibility of malicious DNS servers falsely claiming authority to cause client misconfiguration.

One mitigation for the misconfiguration attack is to use credentials such as CERT resource records within response sets, which TBDS adopted. The document notes that TBDS did not use DNSSEC (DNS Security Extensions), so interactions with DNSSEC-aware servers remain unknown.

Additionally, resolvers must anticipate receiving no replies to some multicast queries when no multicast-enabled servers exist in local scope or when no positive responses are available. Non-response must be treated as a non-cacheable negative response. Since multicast transmission does not provide guaranteed delivery, clients may repeat queries with exponentially increasing intervals, though repeated queries are typically left to the application rather than the resolver.
sections.eli5: Bad people could flood the network with fake answers, or pretend to be a computer they are not. No response might mean no one knows the answer, or it might mean the question never arrived. These problems made the experiment hard to trust.
